name: Pushing a crate across a floor
statement: A worker pushes a crate with a constant horizontal force of $25\ \mathrm{N}$ and the crate slides $4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ in the direction of the force. How much work does the worker do, in J?
solution: For a constant force along the motion, $W = Fd$. So $W = (25)(4.0) = 100\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Rope at an angle
statement: A child drags a sled $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$ along level ground using a rope that makes $30^\circ$ with the horizontal. The tension is $40\ \mathrm{N}$. How much work does the rope do, in J?
solution: Only the component of force along the displacement does work: $W = Fd\cos\theta$. Then $W = (40)(6.0)\cos 30^\circ = 207.8\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Work done by friction
statement: A $20\ \mathrm{kg}$ box slides $5.0\ \mathrm{m}$ across a level floor with coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k = 0.30$. How much work does friction do on the box, in J? (Give the signed value.)
solution: Friction has magnitude $f = \mu_k m g = (0.30)(20)(9.8) = 58.8\ \mathrm{N}$ and points opposite the motion, so its work is negative: $W_f = -fd = -(58.8)(5.0) = -294\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Cart started from rest
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart starts at rest on a frictionless track. A total of $50\ \mathrm{J}$ of work is done on it. What is its final speed, in m/s?
solution: The work-energy theorem gives $W_{\text{net}} = \tfrac12 m v^2 - 0$. So $v = \sqrt{2W/m} = \sqrt{2(50)/2.0} = 7.07\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Braking car
statement: A $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ car traveling at $20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ comes to a complete stop. How much work do the brakes do on the car, in J? (Give the signed value.)
solution: The net work equals the change in kinetic energy: $W = 0 - \tfrac12(1200)(20)^2 = -2.4\times10^5\ \mathrm{J}$. The sign is negative because the car loses kinetic energy.

name: Lifting a bucket
statement: A worker raises a $12\ \mathrm{kg}$ bucket $8.0\ \mathrm{m}$ up a well at constant speed. How much work does the worker do on the bucket, in J?
solution: At constant speed the applied force equals the weight, $mg = 117.6\ \mathrm{N}$, and it acts along the displacement. So $W = mgh = (12)(9.8)(8.0) = 940.8\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Work by gravity on a falling ball
statement: A $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball falls $3.0\ \mathrm{m}$. How much work does gravity do on it, in J?
solution: Gravity points along the displacement, so $W = mgh = (0.50)(9.8)(3.0) = 14.7\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Sliding up a ramp
statement: A $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block is pushed $3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ up a $30^\circ$ incline. How much work does gravity do on the block, in J? (Give the signed value.)
solution: The block rises $h = (3.0)\sin 30^\circ = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$. Gravity opposes the rise, so $W_g = -mgh = -(4.0)(9.8)(1.5) = -58.8\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Speeding up a puck
statement: A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ puck speeds up from $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $10\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the net work done on it, in J?

name: Force opposing motion
statement: A $15\ \mathrm{N}$ force acts on a cart directly opposite to its motion while the cart moves $8.0\ \mathrm{m}$. How much work does this force do, in J?
solution: The angle between force and displacement is $180^\circ$, so $W = Fd\cos180^\circ = -(15)(8.0) = -120\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Area under a force graph
statement: A force acting along the $x$-axis grows linearly as $F = 6x$ (newtons, with $x$ in meters). How much work does it do as an object moves from $x=0$ to $x=3.0\ \mathrm{m}$, in J?
solution: For a variable force, $W = \int F\,dx$, which is the area under the $F$ vs. $x$ graph. Here that area is a triangle of base $3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and height $18\ \mathrm{N}$: $W = \tfrac12(3.0)(18) = 27\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Force that dies away
statement: A cart is pushed along the $x$-axis by $F = 12 - 2x$ (newtons, $x$ in meters). How much work is done from $x=0$ to $x=5.0\ \mathrm{m}$, in J?
solution: $W=\int_0^{5}(12-2x)\,dx = 12(5) - (5)^2 = 60-25 = 35\ \mathrm{J}$. Note the force reverses sign past $x=6\ \mathrm{m}$, but that is outside this range.

name: Cubic force law
statement: A spring-like device exerts $F = 3x^2$ (newtons, $x$ in meters) along the direction of motion. How much work does it do from $x=0$ to $x=2.0\ \mathrm{m}$, in J?

name: Sled with friction and an angled rope
statement: A $30\ \mathrm{kg}$ sled on level ground is pulled $10\ \mathrm{m}$ from rest by a rope with tension $80\ \mathrm{N}$ directed $20^\circ$ above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.10$. What is the sled's final speed, in m/s?
solution: The rope's vertical component lightens the normal force: $N = mg - T\sin\theta = 294 - 27.4 = 266.6\ \mathrm{N}$. Net work is $W = T\cos\theta\, d - \mu_k N d = 751.8 - 266.6 = 485.2\ \mathrm{J}$, so $v = \sqrt{2W/m} = 5.69\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Down a rough incline
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block slides from rest $4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ down a $37^\circ$ incline with $\mu_k = 0.20$. What is its speed at the bottom, in m/s?
solution: Gravity does $mgd\sin\theta = 47.2\ \mathrm{J}$ and friction does $-\mu_k mgd\cos\theta = -12.5\ \mathrm{J}$, for a net $34.7\ \mathrm{J}$. Then $v = \sqrt{2W/m} = \sqrt{34.7} = 5.89\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Compressing a spring
statement: A spring with stiffness $k = 400\ \mathrm{N/m}$ is compressed $0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ from its natural length. How much work does the person doing the compressing perform, in J?
solution: The work stored in a spring is $\tfrac12 k x^2 = \tfrac12(400)(0.15)^2 = 4.5\ \mathrm{J}$. The spring itself does $-4.5\ \mathrm{J}$ on the person's hand.

name: Stopping distance
statement: A $0.40\ \mathrm{kg}$ hockey puck sliding at $12\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is brought to rest by friction with $\mu_k = 0.10$. How far does it travel, in m?
solution: Friction removes all the kinetic energy: $\mu_k m g d = \tfrac12 m v^2$, so $d = v^2/(2\mu_k g)$. The mass cancels: $d = 144/(2 \cdot 0.10 \cdot 9.8) = 73.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Constant-speed haul up a ramp
statement: A $50\ \mathrm{kg}$ crate is pulled $8.0\ \mathrm{m}$ up a $25^\circ$ ramp at constant speed, with $\mu_k = 0.15$ between crate and ramp. How much work does the pulling force (directed up the ramp) do, in J?
solution: At constant speed the pull balances gravity's component and friction: $F = mg(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta) = 490(0.4226 + 0.1360) = 273.7\ \mathrm{N}$. Then $W = Fd = (273.7)(8.0) = 2190\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Elevator cable
statement: An elevator of mass $800\ \mathrm{kg}$ accelerates upward at $1.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ through a height of $10\ \mathrm{m}$. How much work does the cable tension do, in J?
solution: Newton's second law gives $T = m(g+a) = 800(11.3) = 9040\ \mathrm{N}$, directed along the motion. Then $W_T = Td = 9.04\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Bullet in a board
statement: A $10\ \mathrm{g}$ bullet moving at $400\ \mathrm{m/s}$ buries itself $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ into a wooden block that is held fixed. What is the average stopping force, in N?
solution: All the kinetic energy is absorbed over the penetration depth: $\bar F d = \tfrac12 m v^2$. So $\bar F = \tfrac12(0.010)(400)^2/0.060 = 1.33\times10^4\ \mathrm{N}$.

name: Two forces on a box
statement: A $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ box on frictionless ice is acted on by a $30\ \mathrm{N}$ force pointing east and a $12\ \mathrm{N}$ force pointing west. Starting from rest, what is its kinetic energy after moving $7.0\ \mathrm{m}$ east, in J?
solution: The net force is $30-12 = 18\ \mathrm{N}$ east. Net work equals the kinetic energy gained: $K = (18)(7.0) = 126\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Friction on a curved track
statement: A block is dragged around a quarter-circle groove of radius $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ on a horizontal table. A constant friction force of $9.0\ \mathrm{N}$ acts opposite the motion everywhere along the path. How much work does friction do, in J? (Give the signed value.)
solution: Friction always opposes motion, so its work is $-f \times (\text{path length})$, not $-f\times$(straight-line displacement). The arc length is $\tfrac{\pi}{2}(2.0) = 3.14\ \mathrm{m}$, giving $W = -28.3\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Chain hanging off a table
statement: A uniform chain of mass $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and length $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ lies on a frictionless table with $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ of it hanging over the edge. How much work must be done to pull the hanging part back onto the table, in J?
solution: Track the center of mass of the hanging piece. Its mass is $\lambda \ell = (2.0)(0.50) = 1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and its center of mass sits $\ell/2 = 0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ below the tabletop. Raising that piece to the tabletop requires $W = m g (\ell/2) = (1.0)(9.8)(0.25) = 2.45\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Lifting a heavy rope
statement: A uniform rope of mass $6.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and length $3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ hangs from a hook. How much work is needed to reel the whole rope up onto the hook, in J?
solution: The rope's center of mass starts $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ below the hook and ends at the hook. So $W = Mg\,\Delta h_{\rm cm} = (6.0)(9.8)(1.5) = 88.2\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Inverse-square force
statement: A probe moves along the $x$-axis under an attractive force of magnitude $F = 200/x^2$ (newtons, $x$ in meters), directed toward the origin. How much work does this force do as the probe moves from $x = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ to $x = 10\ \mathrm{m}$, in J? (Give the signed value.)
solution: The force points toward the origin while the motion is outward, so the work is negative: $W = -\int_2^{10} \frac{200}{x^2}dx = -\left[\frac{200}{2}-\frac{200}{10}\right] = -80\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Position-dependent friction
statement: A block slides along a track where the coefficient of friction increases with position as $\mu = 0.050\,x$ ($x$ in meters). The block has mass $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and enters at $x = 0$ with speed $6.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. At what value of $x$ does it stop, in m?
solution: Friction work is $\int_0^{X}\mu m g\,dx = 0.025\,m g X^2$. Setting this equal to $\tfrac12 m v^2$, the mass cancels: $X = \sqrt{v^2/(0.05 g)} = \sqrt{36/0.49} = 8.57\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Force along a circular arc
statement: A bead is guided along a circular arc of radius $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ in the $xy$-plane, from the point $(1.5, 0)$ to $(0, 1.5)$, while a constant force $\vec F = (10\ \mathrm{N})\hat x$ acts on it. How much work does $\vec F$ do, in J? (Give the signed value.)
solution: A constant force is conservative, so its work depends only on the endpoints: $W = \vec F\cdot\Delta\vec r$. Here $\Delta \vec r = (-1.5, +1.5)\ \mathrm{m}$, so $W = (10)(-1.5) = -15\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: How far up the ramp?
statement: A block is launched up a $30^\circ$ incline at $8.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$; the coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.25$. How far along the incline does it travel before stopping, in m?
solution: Going up, both gravity and friction remove energy: $\tfrac12 v^2 = g d(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta)$. So $d = \frac{64}{2(9.8)(0.500+0.2165)} = 4.56\ \mathrm{m}$. Mass cancels.

name: Pulling a cart with a rope over a pole
statement: A cart on a frictionless track is pulled by a rope that passes over a smooth pole a height $h = 3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ above the track. Someone pulls the free end of the rope in at a constant $2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. When the cart is $4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ horizontally from the base of the pole, what is the cart's speed, in m/s?
solution: The rope length from cart to pole is $s=\sqrt{h^2+x^2}$, so $\dot s = (x/s)\dot x$. Only the component of the cart's velocity along the rope shortens it. With $s = 5.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and $x = 4.0\ \mathrm{m}$, $|\dot x| = |\dot s|\,s/x = (2.0)(5)/4 = 2.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Chain sliding off a frictionless table
statement: A uniform chain of length $L = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ rests on a frictionless table with a length $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ hanging over the edge. It is released and slides off. What is the speed of the chain at the instant the last link leaves the table, in m/s?
solution: With $y$ hanging, the potential energy is $U = -\tfrac12\lambda g y^2$ (the hanging mass $\lambda y$ with center of mass $y/2$ below the table). Energy conservation gives $\tfrac12 \lambda L v^2 = \tfrac12\lambda g (L^2 - y_0^2)$, so $v = \sqrt{g(L^2-y_0^2)/L} = \sqrt{9.8(4-0.16)/2} = 4.34\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Book on a shelf
statement: A $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ book sits on a shelf $2.2\ \mathrm{m}$ above the floor. Taking the floor as the zero of potential energy, what is the book's gravitational potential energy, in J?
solution: Near Earth's surface $U = mgh$, so $U = (1.5)(9.8)(2.2) = 32.3\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Stretching a spring
statement: A spring of stiffness $k = 250\ \mathrm{N/m}$ is stretched $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$. How much elastic potential energy is stored, in J?

name: Doubling the stretch
statement: A spring stores $3.0\ \mathrm{J}$ when stretched by $x$. How much does it store when stretched by $2x$, in J?
solution: Spring energy goes as $x^2$, so doubling the stretch quadruples the energy: $4(3.0) = 12\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Climbing stairs
statement: A $60\ \mathrm{kg}$ student climbs a flight of $18$ stairs, each $0.18\ \mathrm{m}$ high. How much gravitational potential energy does the student gain, in J?
solution: The total rise is $18(0.18) = 3.24\ \mathrm{m}$, so $\Delta U = mgh = (60)(9.8)(3.24) = 1905\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Dropping below the reference point
statement: A $0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ stone is dropped from ground level into a well and falls $12\ \mathrm{m}$. Taking ground level as $U=0$, what is its potential energy at the bottom, in J?
solution: Below the reference point the potential energy is negative: $U = -mgh = -(0.80)(9.8)(12) = -94.1\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Force from a linear potential
statement: A particle moves along the $x$-axis in a potential $U(x) = 5x$ (joules, $x$ in meters). What is the force on the particle, in N? (Give the signed value.)
solution: $F = -dU/dx = -5\ \mathrm{N}$: a constant force pointing toward $-x$, downhill in the potential.

name: Force from a quadratic potential
statement: A particle sits in the potential $U(x) = 40x^2$ (joules, $x$ in meters). What is the magnitude of the force on it at $x = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}$, in N?
solution: $F = -dU/dx = -80x$, so at $x = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ the magnitude is $24\ \mathrm{N}$ pointing back toward the origin. This is a spring with $k = 80\ \mathrm{N/m}$.

name: Equilibrium of a hanging mass
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass hangs at rest from a spring with $k = 140\ \mathrm{N/m}$. By how much is the spring stretched, in m?
solution: At equilibrium the spring force balances the weight: $kx = mg$, so $x = (2.0)(9.8)/140 = 0.14\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Ramp versus stairs
statement: A $25\ \mathrm{kg}$ box is carried to a loading dock $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$ high, once straight up and once along a $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$ ramp. What is the change in gravitational potential energy along the ramp, in J?
solution: Gravity is conservative, so $\Delta U$ depends only on the height change, not the path: $\Delta U = (25)(9.8)(1.2) = 294\ \mathrm{J}$ either way.

name: Two springs, same force
statement: A spring with $k = 800\ \mathrm{N/m}$ is compressed until it pushes back with $60\ \mathrm{N}$. How much energy is stored, in J?

name: Pendulum height
statement: A $0.30\ \mathrm{kg}$ pendulum bob on a $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$ string is pulled aside until the string makes $40^\circ$ with the vertical. How much gravitational potential energy has it gained relative to the lowest point, in J?
solution: The bob rises $h = \ell(1-\cos\theta) = 1.2(1-0.766) = 0.281\ \mathrm{m}$. Then $\Delta U = mgh = (0.30)(9.8)(0.281) = 0.826\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Springs in series
statement: Two springs, $k_1 = 300\ \mathrm{N/m}$ and $k_2 = 600\ \mathrm{N/m}$, are joined end to end and the combination is stretched by a $90\ \mathrm{N}$ pull. What is the total stored energy, in J?
solution: Springs in series share the same tension, so the effective stiffness is $k_{\rm eff} = (1/300+1/600)^{-1} = 200\ \mathrm{N/m}$. Then $U = F^2/(2k_{\rm eff}) = 8100/400 = 20.25\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Springs in parallel
statement: Two springs, $k_1 = 250\ \mathrm{N/m}$ and $k_2 = 150\ \mathrm{N/m}$, are attached side by side to the same block and both are stretched $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$. What is the total stored energy, in J?
solution: Side-by-side springs share the same stretch, so stiffnesses add: $k_{\rm eff} = 400\ \mathrm{N/m}$. Then $U = \tfrac12(400)(0.10)^2 = 2.0\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Reading a potential energy curve
statement: A particle moves in the potential $U(x) = 2x^3 - 12x$ (joules, $x$ in meters). At what positive $x$ is the particle in equilibrium, in m?
solution: Equilibrium means zero force, i.e. $dU/dx = 0$: $6x^2 - 12 = 0$, so $x = \sqrt{2} = 1.414\ \mathrm{m}$. Since $U'' = 12x > 0$ there, this is a stable minimum.

name: Depth of a potential well
statement: A particle moves in $U(x) = 2x^3 - 12x$ (joules, $x$ in meters). What is the value of $U$ at the stable equilibrium point, in J?
solution: The stable point is $x=\sqrt2$. Then $U = 2(2\sqrt2) - 12\sqrt2 = -8\sqrt2 = -11.3\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Spring gun
statement: A toy gun's spring ($k = 500\ \mathrm{N/m}$) is compressed $8.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and fires a $20\ \mathrm{g}$ dart horizontally. Assuming no losses, what is the dart's launch speed, in m/s?
solution: All the spring energy becomes kinetic: $\tfrac12 k x^2 = \tfrac12 m v^2$. Then $v = x\sqrt{k/m} = 0.08\sqrt{500/0.020} = 12.6\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Escaping a well
statement: A $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ particle sits at the bottom of a potential well where $U = -30\ \mathrm{J}$; the well's rim is at $U = -6\ \mathrm{J}$. What is the minimum speed it needs at the bottom to escape over the rim, in m/s?
solution: It needs kinetic energy at least equal to the depth below the rim: $\tfrac12 m v^2 \geq 24\ \mathrm{J}$. So $v = \sqrt{2(24)/0.50} = 9.80\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Vertical spring with a mass
statement: A $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block is placed gently on top of a vertical spring ($k = 200\ \mathrm{N/m}$) and released from rest at the spring's natural length. What is the maximum compression, in m?
solution: At maximum compression the block is momentarily at rest, so $mgx = \tfrac12 kx^2$, giving $x = 2mg/k = 2(9.8)/200 = 0.098\ \mathrm{m}$. Note this is twice the equilibrium sag.

name: Is this force conservative?
statement: A force acting along a loop does $+18\ \mathrm{J}$ on the outbound leg and $-18\ \mathrm{J}$ on the return leg of a closed path. What is the total work around the closed loop, in J?
solution: A conservative force does zero net work around any closed path, and that is exactly what these numbers show: $18 + (-18) = 0\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Potential of a stretched rubber band
statement: A rubber band resists stretching with force $F = 80x + 400x^3$ (newtons, $x$ in meters). How much potential energy is stored at $x = 0.20\ \mathrm{m}$, in J?

name: Force from a 2D potential
statement: A particle moves in $U(x,y) = 3x^2 + 5y^2$ (joules, meters). What is the magnitude of the force at the point $(1.0, 1.0)$, in N?
solution: The force is $\vec F = -\nabla U = (-6x, -10y)$. At $(1,1)$ this is $(-6,-10)\ \mathrm{N}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{36+100} = 11.7\ \mathrm{N}$.

name: Gravity far from Earth
statement: Using $U = -GMm/r$ with $GM_\oplus = 3.986\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, how much energy is needed to move a $500\ \mathrm{kg}$ satellite from a circular orbit of radius $7.0\times10^6\ \mathrm{m}$ to one of radius $1.4\times10^7\ \mathrm{m}$? Consider only the change in potential energy, in J.
solution: $\Delta U = -GMm\left(\frac{1}{r_2}-\frac{1}{r_1}\right) = GMm\left(\frac{1}{r_1}-\frac{1}{r_2}\right)$. With the numbers, $\Delta U = (3.986\times10^{14})(500)(1/7.0\times10^6 - 1/1.4\times10^7) = 1.42\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Turning points in a well
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ particle moves in $U(x) = 4x^2 - x^4$ (joules, $x$ in meters) with total energy $3.0\ \mathrm{J}$, starting near $x=0$. What is the positive turning point, in m?
solution: At a turning point $K=0$, so $U(x)=E$: $4x^2-x^4 = 3$. With $u = x^2$, $u^2-4u+3=0$ gives $u=1$ or $u=3$. Starting near the origin the particle first reaches $u=1$, i.e. $x = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Barrier height
statement: For $U(x) = 4x^2 - x^4$ (joules, meters), the potential rises then falls. What is the maximum value of $U$ for $x>0$, in J?
solution: Set $U' = 8x - 4x^3 = 0$, giving $x^2 = 2$. Then $U = 4(2) - (2)^2 = 4.0\ \mathrm{J}$. A particle with more energy than this escapes to large $x$.

name: Small oscillations in a well
statement: A $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ particle sits at the minimum of $U(x) = 6x^2 + 2x^4$ (joules, meters). What is the angular frequency of small oscillations about $x=0$, in rad/s?
solution: Near $x=0$ the quartic term is negligible and $U \approx 6x^2$, an effective spring with $k = U''(0) = 12\ \mathrm{N/m}$. Then $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{12/0.50} = 4.90\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

name: Lennard-Jones minimum
statement: Two atoms interact through the Lennard-Jones potential $U(r) = \frac{A}{r^{12}} - \frac{B}{r^{6}}$, with $A = 2.0$ and $B = 4.0$ in SI units (joules times the appropriate power of meters). At what separation $r$ is the potential energy a minimum, in m?
solution: Set $dU/dr = -12A r^{-13} + 6B r^{-7} = 0$, which gives $r^6 = 2A/B$. With $A=2.0$ and $B=4.0$, $r^6 = 1.0$ and $r = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Bungee jumper
statement: A $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ jumper steps off a bridge attached to a bungee cord of unstretched length $20\ \mathrm{m}$ and stiffness $60\ \mathrm{N/m}$. How far below the bridge is the lowest point of the fall, in m?
solution: Set gravitational energy released equal to cord energy stored: $mgd = \tfrac12 k(d-20)^2$, i.e. $686d = 30(d-20)^2$. This is $30d^2 - 1886d + 12000 = 0$, whose physical root is $d = 55.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Force curve to energy
statement: A conservative force along $x$ is $F(x) = -kx + \beta x^2$ with $k = 20\ \mathrm{N/m}$ and $\beta = 30\ \mathrm{N/m^2}$. Taking $U(0)=0$, what is $U$ at $x = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$, in J?

name: Tunnel through the Earth
statement: Inside a uniform sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$, the gravitational force on a mass $m$ at radius $r$ is $F = GMmr/R^3$ toward the center. Taking $U=0$ at the center, how much potential energy does a $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass have at the surface of the Earth's model sphere, where $g_{\rm surf} = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $R = 6.37\times10^6\ \mathrm{m}$, in J?
solution: Since $GM/R^3 = g_{\rm surf}/R$, the force is $F = m g_{\rm surf} r/R$: a spring with $k = mg_{\rm surf}/R$. So $U(R) = \tfrac12 k R^2 = \tfrac12 m g_{\rm surf} R = \tfrac12(1.0)(9.8)(6.37\times10^6) = 3.12\times10^7\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Stability of a magnet above a coil
statement: A small magnet on a vertical rod has potential energy $U(z) = \frac{C}{z^2} + mgz$ with $C = 0.020\ \mathrm{J\,m^2}$ and $m = 0.10\ \mathrm{kg}$. At what height $z$ does it float in equilibrium, in m?
solution: Equilibrium requires $dU/dz = -2C/z^3 + mg = 0$, so $z = (2C/mg)^{1/3} = (0.040/0.98)^{1/3} = 0.345\ \mathrm{m}$. Since $U'' = 6C/z^4 > 0$, the float point is stable.

name: Dropped stone
statement: A stone is dropped from rest from a height of $5.0\ \mathrm{m}$. What is its speed just before hitting the ground, in m/s?
solution: $mgh = \tfrac12 mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{98} = 9.90\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Mass cancels.

name: Frictionless slide
statement: A child of mass $25\ \mathrm{kg}$ starts from rest at the top of a frictionless slide $3.2\ \mathrm{m}$ high. What is her speed at the bottom, in m/s?
solution: Only the height matters on a frictionless slide: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{62.7} = 7.92\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Ball thrown straight up
statement: A ball is thrown straight up at $14\ \mathrm{m/s}$. How high does it rise, in m?
solution: At the top all kinetic energy has become potential: $h = v^2/(2g) = 196/19.6 = 10.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Pendulum swing
statement: A pendulum bob is released from rest at a height $0.45\ \mathrm{m}$ above its lowest point. What is its speed at the lowest point, in m/s?
solution: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{8.82} = 2.97\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The string does no work since it is always perpendicular to the motion.

name: Skateboarder in a bowl
statement: A skateboarder enters the bottom of a frictionless bowl at $8.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. How high up the wall does she rise, in m?

name: Spring launches a block
statement: A spring with $k = 600\ \mathrm{N/m}$ is compressed $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$ and released against a $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless table. What is the block's speed after it leaves the spring, in m/s?
solution: $\tfrac12 kx^2 = \tfrac12 mv^2$, so $v = x\sqrt{k/m} = 0.10\sqrt{1200} = 3.46\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Halfway down
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball is dropped from $8.0\ \mathrm{m}$. What is its kinetic energy when it has fallen $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$, in J?
solution: Kinetic energy equals the potential energy lost: $K = mg(6.0) = (2.0)(9.8)(6.0) = 117.6\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Rough floor stop
statement: A $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block slides down a frictionless ramp from $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ high, then crosses a rough floor with $\mu_k = 0.40$. How far does it slide on the floor, in m?
solution: All the energy $mgh$ is eaten by friction: $mgh = \mu_k mg d$, so $d = h/\mu_k = 2.0/0.40 = 5.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Both mass and $g$ cancel.

name: Speed at a lower point on a track
statement: A cart starts from rest at height $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$ on a frictionless track and passes over a hill of height $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$. What is its speed at the top of that hill, in m/s?
solution: Only the net drop counts: $v = \sqrt{2g(6.0-2.0)} = \sqrt{78.4} = 8.85\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Energy lost in a bounce
statement: A $0.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball dropped from $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ rebounds to $1.1\ \mathrm{m}$. How much mechanical energy was lost, in J?
solution: The loss is the drop in gravitational potential energy between the two high points: $mg\Delta h = (0.20)(9.8)(0.40) = 0.784\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Loop-the-loop minimum speed
statement: A cart on a frictionless track runs through a vertical loop of radius $2.5\ \mathrm{m}$. From what minimum height above the bottom of the loop must it be released to stay on the track, in m?
solution: At the top the minimum condition is that gravity alone supplies the centripetal force: $v_{\rm top}^2 = gR$. Energy conservation gives $gh = \tfrac12 v_{\rm top}^2 + g(2R)$, so $h = 2.5R = 6.25\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Ski jump landing speed
statement: A skier leaves a ramp $15\ \mathrm{m}$ above the landing area at $12\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Ignoring air resistance, what is her speed on landing, in m/s?
solution: Energy conservation gives $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2gh$, independent of launch angle: $v = \sqrt{144 + 294} = 20.9\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Block, spring, and rough patch
statement: A $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ block is pushed against a spring ($k = 900\ \mathrm{N/m}$) compressed $0.12\ \mathrm{m}$ and released. It then crosses a $0.80\ \mathrm{m}$ rough patch with $\mu_k = 0.25$. What is its speed after the patch, in m/s?
solution: The spring supplies $\tfrac12 kx^2 = 6.48\ \mathrm{J}$; friction removes $\mu_k mgd = 2.94\ \mathrm{J}$. The remaining $3.54\ \mathrm{J}$ is kinetic, so $v = \sqrt{2(3.54)/1.5} = 2.17\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Pendulum with a peg
statement: A bob on a $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ string is released from horizontal. What is the tension in the string at the lowest point, expressed as a multiple of the bob's weight? (Give the pure number.)
solution: At the bottom $v^2 = 2g\ell$. Then $T - mg = mv^2/\ell = 2mg$, so $T = 3mg$. The answer is $3$, independent of mass and length.

name: Two-stage drop
statement: A $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ box slides $3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ down a frictionless $30^\circ$ ramp and then $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ along a level floor with $\mu_k = 0.30$. What is its speed at the end, in m/s?
solution: The ramp drop is $h = 3.0\sin30^\circ = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$, releasing $mgh = 58.8\ \mathrm{J}$. Friction on the floor removes $\mu_k mgd = 23.5\ \mathrm{J}$, leaving $35.3\ \mathrm{J}$. Then $v = \sqrt{2(35.3)/4.0} = 4.20\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Water slide with friction
statement: A $55\ \mathrm{kg}$ rider descends $9.0\ \mathrm{m}$ on a slide and arrives at the bottom moving at $11\ \mathrm{m/s}$. How much energy was dissipated by friction, in J?
solution: Potential energy released is $mgh = 4851\ \mathrm{J}$; kinetic energy gained is $\tfrac12 mv^2 = 3327.5\ \mathrm{J}$. The difference, $1523.5\ \mathrm{J}$, went to friction.

name: Vertical spring launch
statement: A $0.25\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball rests on a vertical spring ($k = 320\ \mathrm{N/m}$) that is compressed $0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ below its natural length. When released, how high above the release point does the ball rise, in m?
solution: The spring energy $\tfrac12 kx^2 = 3.6\ \mathrm{J}$ becomes gravitational energy: $h = 3.6/(0.25\cdot 9.8) = 1.47\ \mathrm{m}$ above the release point.

name: Cart over a bump
statement: A cart starts from rest at the top of a frictionless hill $5.0\ \mathrm{m}$ high and crosses a circular bump of radius $8.0\ \mathrm{m}$ whose crest is $3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ above the bottom. Is it still on the track? Give the ratio $v^2/(gR)$ at the crest as a pure number.
solution: At the crest $v^2 = 2g(5.0-3.0) = 39.2\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}$, and $gR = 78.4$. The ratio is $0.50$; since it is less than $1$, gravity is more than enough to curve the cart and it stays on the track.

name: Marble in a hemispherical bowl
statement: A marble is released from the rim of a frictionless hemispherical bowl of radius $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. What is the normal force on the marble at the bottom, as a multiple of its weight? (Give the pure number.)
solution: At the bottom $v^2 = 2gR$, so $N - mg = mv^2/R = 2mg$ and $N = 3mg$. The answer is $3$, independent of $R$.

name: Chain of energy transformations
statement: A $0.60\ \mathrm{kg}$ block slides down a frictionless $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$ drop and then compresses a spring of stiffness $1500\ \mathrm{N/m}$. What is the maximum compression, in m?
solution: All the gravitational energy $mgh = 7.056\ \mathrm{J}$ goes into the spring: $x = \sqrt{2mgh/k} = \sqrt{2(7.056)/1500} = 0.0970\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Escape from a rough hill
statement: A $12\ \mathrm{kg}$ sled is pushed up a $20^\circ$ slope at $9.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$; $\mu_k = 0.12$. It slides up, stops, and slides back down. What is its speed when it returns to the start, in m/s?
solution: Going up, $d = v_0^2/[2g(\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta)] = 81/(2\cdot9.8\cdot0.4548) = 9.09\ \mathrm{m}$. Coming down, friction now helps gravity less: $v^2 = 2gd(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta) = 2(9.8)(9.09)(0.2293)$, so $v = 6.39\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Roller coaster with drag
statement: A $500\ \mathrm{kg}$ coaster car drops $40\ \mathrm{m}$ and reaches $25\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What fraction of the released potential energy was lost to friction and drag? (Give the pure number.)
solution: Released energy: $mgh = 1.96\times10^5\ \mathrm{J}$. Kinetic energy gained: $\tfrac12 mv^2 = 1.5625\times10^5\ \mathrm{J}$. The lost fraction is $1 - 1.5625/1.96 = 0.203$.

name: Block sliding off a sphere
statement: A small block slides from rest off the top of a frictionless sphere of radius $R = 1.6\ \mathrm{m}$. At what height above the center of the sphere does it lose contact, in m?
solution: Contact is lost when $N=0$, so gravity's radial component supplies the centripetal force: $mg\cos\theta = mv^2/R$. Energy conservation gives $v^2 = 2gR(1-\cos\theta)$. Combining, $\cos\theta = 2/3$, so the height above the center is $R\cos\theta = 2R/3 = 1.07\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Speed leaving the sphere
statement: A block slides from rest off a frictionless sphere of radius $2.4\ \mathrm{m}$. What is its speed at the moment it leaves the surface, in m/s?
solution: Leaving happens at $\cos\theta = 2/3$, where $v^2 = gR\cos\theta = 2gR/3$. So $v = \sqrt{2(9.8)(2.4)/3} = 3.96\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Minimum push for a loop with friction
statement: A $0.40\ \mathrm{kg}$ bead must complete a vertical loop of radius $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$. Friction dissipates $0.30\ \mathrm{J}$ between the bottom of the loop and the top. What minimum speed must it have at the bottom, in m/s?
solution: At the top, minimum condition $v_{\rm top}^2 = gR = 4.9\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}$. Energy: $\tfrac12 mv_b^2 = \tfrac12 mv_{\rm top}^2 + mg(2R) + 0.30\ \mathrm{J}$, so $v_b^2 = 4.9 + 19.6 + 1.5 = 26.0$ and $v_b = 5.10\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Two blocks and a pulley
statement: A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless table is connected over a massless pulley to a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ hanging block. Starting from rest, what is their common speed after the hanging block descends $0.80\ \mathrm{m}$, in m/s?
solution: The falling block releases $m_2 g h = 15.68\ \mathrm{J}$, shared as kinetic energy by both blocks (they move at the same speed): $\tfrac12(m_1+m_2)v^2 = 15.68$. So $v = \sqrt{2(15.68)/5.0} = 2.50\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Spring and incline combination
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block is released from rest on a $35^\circ$ incline, slides $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ down against $\mu_k = 0.20$, and then compresses a spring ($k = 2000\ \mathrm{N/m}$) mounted along the incline. What is the maximum compression, in m? (Include the extra descent during compression.)
solution: Let $x$ be the compression. Over the total travel $1.5+x$, the block gains $mg(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)(1.5+x)$ and stores $\tfrac12 kx^2$. With $mg(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta) = 8.03\ \mathrm{N}$, solve $1000x^2 - 8.03x - 12.04 = 0$, giving $x = 0.114\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Rope swing over water
statement: A $60\ \mathrm{kg}$ swinger grabs a $5.0\ \mathrm{m}$ rope at $50^\circ$ from vertical, swings down, and lets go at the lowest point, $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ above the water. What is her speed when she hits the water, in m/s?
solution: She drops $h = 5.0(1-\cos50^\circ) = 1.786\ \mathrm{m}$ on the rope, then $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ in free flight. Since the rope does no work and gravity is conservative, $v = \sqrt{2g(3.786)} = 8.62\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Sliding wedge
statement: A $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block slides down a frictionless $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ wedge of height $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$; the wedge is free to slide on a frictionless floor. What is the block's speed relative to the ground when it reaches the bottom, in m/s? (The block moves horizontally at the bottom.)
solution: Horizontal momentum stays zero: $m v_1 = M v_2$. Energy: $\tfrac12 m v_1^2 + \tfrac12 M v_2^2 = mgh$. Substituting $v_2 = (m/M)v_1$ gives $v_1^2(1+m/M) = 2gh$, so $v_1 = \sqrt{2(9.8)(0.60)/1.25} = 3.07\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Hanging chain released
statement: A uniform chain of length $1.8\ \mathrm{m}$ is held straight along a frictionless table with one end just at the edge. It is released and slides off (the leading end falls straight down along the table edge, guided by a smooth peg). What is the chain's speed when the last link leaves the table, in m/s?
solution: With $y$ hanging, $U = -\tfrac12\lambda g y^2$. Starting at $y\approx0$ and ending at $y=L$, energy conservation gives $\tfrac12 \lambda L v^2 = \tfrac12 \lambda g L^2$, so $v = \sqrt{gL} = \sqrt{17.64} = 4.20\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Lifting boxes
statement: A worker lifts a $15\ \mathrm{kg}$ box $1.4\ \mathrm{m}$ onto a shelf in $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the average power output, in W?

name: Light bulb energy
statement: A $60\ \mathrm{W}$ bulb runs for $5.0$ hours. How much energy does it use, in J?
solution: $E = Pt = (60)(5\times3600\ \mathrm{s}) = 1.08\times10^6\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Cyclist against drag
statement: A cyclist rides at a steady $8.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ against a total resistive force of $25\ \mathrm{N}$. What power must she supply, in W?
solution: At constant speed the drive force equals the resistance, so $P = Fv = (25)(8.0) = 200\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Elevator motor
statement: An elevator lifts $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ at a constant $2.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What power does the motor deliver, in W?
solution: At constant speed the tension is $mg = 9800\ \mathrm{N}$, so $P = Fv = (9800)(2.5) = 2.45\times10^4\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Stair-climb power
statement: A $65\ \mathrm{kg}$ runner climbs $12\ \mathrm{m}$ of stairs in $9.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the average power, in W?

name: Water pump
statement: A pump raises $200\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water $18\ \mathrm{m}$ every minute. What is its output power, in W?

name: Power to accelerate a car
statement: A $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ car goes from rest to $20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ in $8.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the average power delivered, in W?
solution: $P_{\rm avg} = \Delta K/t = \tfrac12(1000)(400)/8.0 = 2.5\times10^4\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Horsepower conversion
statement: An engine is rated at $150$ horsepower ($1\ \mathrm{hp} = 746\ \mathrm{W}$). What is its power in W?
solution: $P = 150 \times 746 = 1.119\times10^5\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Force from power and speed
statement: A locomotive delivers $1.2\ \mathrm{MW}$ at $30\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the driving force, in N?
solution: $F = P/v = 1.2\times10^6/30 = 4.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{N}$.

name: Instantaneous power of a falling ball
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball has fallen for $3.0\ \mathrm{s}$ from rest. What is the instantaneous power delivered by gravity at that moment, in W?
solution: Its speed is $v = gt = 29.4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and gravity acts along $v$, so $P = mgv = (2.0)(9.8)(29.4) = 576\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Average versus instantaneous power
statement: A $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ car accelerates uniformly from rest to $24\ \mathrm{m/s}$ in $10\ \mathrm{s}$ on a level frictionless road. What is the instantaneous power at $t = 10\ \mathrm{s}$, in W?
solution: The acceleration is $a = 2.4\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, so the force is $F = ma = 2880\ \mathrm{N}$ and at $t=10\ \mathrm{s}$, $v = 24\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Then $P = Fv = 6.91\times10^4\ \mathrm{W}$ — exactly twice the average power, as it must be for uniform acceleration.

name: Top speed from engine power
statement: A car's engine delivers $60\ \mathrm{kW}$ to the wheels. Drag and rolling resistance total $F = 0.80 v^2$ (newtons, $v$ in m/s). What is the car's top speed, in m/s?
solution: Top speed is where all the power goes to fighting resistance: $P = Fv = 0.80v^3$. So $v = (60000/0.80)^{1/3} = 42.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Doubling top speed
statement: With drag proportional to $v^2$, the power needed at top speed goes as $v^3$. If a boat needs $20\ \mathrm{kW}$ to cruise at $10\ \mathrm{m/s}$, what power is needed at $15\ \mathrm{m/s}$, in W?

name: Power up a hill
statement: A $1400\ \mathrm{kg}$ car climbs a $6.0^\circ$ incline at a steady $22\ \mathrm{m/s}$, with $700\ \mathrm{N}$ of drag. What power must the engine deliver, in W?
solution: The engine must overcome gravity's component and drag: $F = mg\sin\theta + F_d = 1434 + 700 = 2134\ \mathrm{N}$. Then $P = Fv = (2134)(22) = 4.70\times10^4\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Power delivered by a spring
statement: A block attached to a spring ($k = 400\ \mathrm{N/m}$) is at $x = 0.10\ \mathrm{m}$ moving toward the origin at $1.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the instantaneous power delivered by the spring, in W?
solution: The spring force is $kx = 40\ \mathrm{N}$ pointing toward the origin, in the same direction as $v$, so $P = Fv = (40)(1.5) = 60\ \mathrm{W}$ (positive: the spring is speeding the block up).

name: Time-varying power
statement: A motor's output rises linearly as $P = 300t$ watts for the first $10\ \mathrm{s}$. How much total energy does it deliver in that interval, in J?

name: Constant-power start
statement: A $900\ \mathrm{kg}$ car's engine delivers a constant $45\ \mathrm{kW}$. Neglecting friction and starting from rest, how long does it take to reach $25\ \mathrm{m/s}$, in s?
solution: With constant power, the work done equals $Pt$, and all of it becomes kinetic energy: $Pt = \tfrac12 mv^2$. So $t = \tfrac12(900)(625)/45000 = 6.25\ \mathrm{s}$.

name: Speed under constant power
statement: A $900\ \mathrm{kg}$ car with constant power $45\ \mathrm{kW}$ starts from rest on a frictionless road. What is its speed after $3.0\ \mathrm{s}$, in m/s?
solution: $Pt = \tfrac12 mv^2$ gives $v = \sqrt{2Pt/m} = \sqrt{2(45000)(3)/900} = 17.3\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Note $v \propto \sqrt{t}$, so acceleration falls off.

name: Human metabolic power
statement: A cyclist's body burns energy at $600\ \mathrm{W}$ but converts only $22\%$ of it to mechanical work. What mechanical power does she produce, in W?
solution: $P_{\rm mech} = \eta P_{\rm in} = (0.22)(600) = 132\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Hydroelectric dam
statement: Water flows over a dam at $500\ \mathrm{kg/s}$ from a height of $60\ \mathrm{m}$, and the turbines are $85\%$ efficient. What electrical power is produced, in W?
solution: The gravitational power available is $\dot m g h = (500)(9.8)(60) = 2.94\times10^5\ \mathrm{W}$. At $85\%$ efficiency the output is $2.50\times10^5\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Wind on a sail
statement: A sailboat is pushed by a $340\ \mathrm{N}$ force directed $35^\circ$ from the boat's velocity, and the boat moves at $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the power delivered, in W?
solution: $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v = Fv\cos\theta = (340)(4.0)\cos35^\circ = 1114\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Braking power
statement: A $1500\ \mathrm{kg}$ truck slows from $30\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to $10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ in $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$. At what average rate do the brakes dissipate energy, in W?
solution: The kinetic energy lost is $\tfrac12(1500)(900-100) = 6.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{J}$, over $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$: $P = 1.2\times10^5\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Distance under constant power
statement: A $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ car with constant power $50\ \mathrm{kW}$ starts from rest on a frictionless road. How far does it travel in the first $8.0\ \mathrm{s}$, in m?
solution: From $Pt = \tfrac12 mv^2$, $v = \sqrt{2P/m}\,\sqrt{t}$. Integrating, $x = \tfrac23\sqrt{2P/m}\,t^{3/2} = \tfrac23(10)(22.6) = 150.8\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Grain falling onto a belt
statement: Grain falls vertically onto a horizontal conveyor belt at $12\ \mathrm{kg/s}$; the belt moves at $2.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What power must the motor supply to keep the belt at constant speed, in W?
solution: The force needed is $F = \dot m v = (12)(2.5) = 30\ \mathrm{N}$, so $P = Fv = \dot m v^2 = 75\ \mathrm{W}$. Only half of this, $37.5\ \mathrm{W}$, ends up as grain kinetic energy; the rest is lost to sliding friction as each grain is accelerated.

name: Energy wasted accelerating grain
statement: Grain falls onto a belt moving at $2.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at a rate of $12\ \mathrm{kg/s}$. At what rate is energy dissipated by friction between grain and belt, in W?
solution: The motor supplies $\dot m v^2 = 75\ \mathrm{W}$ but the grain's kinetic energy grows at only $\tfrac12\dot m v^2 = 37.5\ \mathrm{W}$. The missing $37.5\ \mathrm{W}$ is dissipated by the sliding.

name: Rowing boat power scaling
statement: A boat needs power $P = bv^3$ to move. A rower producing $180\ \mathrm{W}$ reaches $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Two identical rowers in the same-drag boat produce $360\ \mathrm{W}$ total. What is their speed, in m/s?
solution: Since $P\propto v^3$, doubling the power multiplies speed by $2^{1/3} = 1.26$: $v = 3.0(1.26) = 3.78\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Racing speed is very expensive in power.

name: Chain being lifted at constant speed
statement: A uniform chain of linear density $2.0\ \mathrm{kg/m}$ lies coiled on the floor. One end is raised at a constant $1.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the power needed at the moment $3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ of chain is off the floor? Include only the weight of the lifted chain, in W.
solution: The lifted weight is $\lambda y g = (2.0)(3.0)(9.8) = 58.8\ \mathrm{N}$, moving at $1.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$, so $P = 88.2\ \mathrm{W}$. (A full treatment adds a small term $\lambda v^3$ for accelerating new links.)

name: Peak power during a jump
statement: A $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ athlete pushes off the ground with a constant force so that she leaves the ground at $3.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ after her center of mass rises $0.45\ \mathrm{m}$ during the push. What is her peak (take-off instant) mechanical power, in W?
solution: The push acceleration is $a = v^2/(2d) = 10.24/0.90 = 11.38\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, so the ground force is $F = m(g+a) = 70(21.18) = 1482\ \mathrm{N}$. Peak power occurs at take-off when $v = 3.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$: $P = Fv = 4743\ \mathrm{W}$.

name: Terminal speed of a power-limited car with linear drag
statement: A car's engine gives constant power $P = 30\ \mathrm{kW}$ and drag is $F = cv$ with $c = 12\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}$. What is the top speed, in m/s?
solution: Top speed occurs when $P = Fv = cv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{P/c} = \sqrt{2500} = 50\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Time to reach 90% of top speed
statement: A car of mass $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ has constant power $30\ \mathrm{kW}$ and linear drag $F = 12v$ (SI). Its top speed is $50\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Starting from rest, how long does it take to reach $45\ \mathrm{m/s}$, in s?
solution: Newton's law gives $mv\frac{dv}{dt} = P - cv^2$. Separating and integrating with $v_t^2 = P/c$: $t = \frac{m}{2c}\ln\!\frac{v_t^2}{v_t^2-v^2}$. With the numbers, $t = 41.67\ln(2500/475) = 69.2\ \mathrm{s}$. The last few m/s take most of the time.

name: Momentum of a runner
statement: A $72\ \mathrm{kg}$ runner moves at $6.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is his momentum, in kg·m/s?

name: Impulse from a constant force
statement: A $40\ \mathrm{N}$ force acts on a cart for $0.25\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the impulse delivered, in N·s?
solution: For a constant force, $J = F\Delta t = (40)(0.25) = 10\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

name: Change in momentum of a ball
statement: A $0.15\ \mathrm{kg}$ baseball moving at $30\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is caught and stopped. What is the magnitude of the impulse on the ball, in N·s?

name: Bouncing ball reverses
statement: A $0.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball hits a wall at $8.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and rebounds at $6.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the impulse on the ball, in N·s?
solution: The velocity reverses direction, so the change is $6.0-(-8.0) = 14\ \mathrm{m/s}$ in magnitude. Then $|J| = (0.20)(14) = 2.8\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ — much larger than for a ball that simply stops.

name: Average force in a catch
statement: A $0.25\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball travelling at $20\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is stopped over $0.080\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the average force, in N?
solution: $\bar F = \Delta p/\Delta t = (0.25)(20)/0.080 = 62.5\ \mathrm{N}$.

name: Rocket thrust
statement: A rocket engine ejects $3.0\ \mathrm{kg/s}$ of exhaust at $2500\ \mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the rocket. What is the thrust, in N?
solution: Thrust is the rate of momentum ejection: $F = \dot m v_{\rm ex} = (3.0)(2500) = 7500\ \mathrm{N}$.

name: Momentum and kinetic energy
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ object has kinetic energy $36\ \mathrm{J}$. What is its momentum, in kg·m/s?

name: Cart pushed for a while
statement: A $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart at rest on frictionless ground is pushed by a constant $18\ \mathrm{N}$ for $4.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What is its final speed, in m/s?
solution: $J = F\Delta t = 72\ \mathrm{N\,s} = mv$, so $v = 72/5.0 = 14.4\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Gravity as an impulse
statement: A $0.60\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball is in free flight for $1.8\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the magnitude of the impulse gravity delivers, in N·s?
solution: $J = mg\Delta t = (0.60)(9.8)(1.8) = 10.6\ \mathrm{N\,s}$, directed downward.

name: Water jet on a wall
statement: A hose sprays water at $4.0\ \mathrm{kg/s}$ horizontally at $15\ \mathrm{m/s}$ against a wall, where it drops straight down without rebounding. What force does the water exert on the wall, in N?
solution: The water's horizontal momentum is destroyed at a rate $\dot m v = (4.0)(15) = 60\ \mathrm{N}$, which is the force on the wall.

name: Force-time graph
statement: A force on a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ puck rises linearly from $0$ to $60\ \mathrm{N}$ over $0.10\ \mathrm{s}$, then falls linearly back to $0$ over the next $0.10\ \mathrm{s}$. If the puck starts at rest, what is its final speed, in m/s?
solution: The impulse is the area under the $F$-$t$ graph: a triangle of base $0.20\ \mathrm{s}$ and height $60\ \mathrm{N}$, so $J = 6.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. Then $v = J/m = 3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Time-varying force
statement: A force $F(t) = 30t - 5t^2$ (newtons, $t$ in seconds) acts on a $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block, initially at rest, from $t=0$ to $t=6.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the block's final speed, in m/s?

name: Egg on a pillow
statement: A $0.055\ \mathrm{kg}$ egg falls $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$ and is stopped by a pillow over $0.15\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the average force the pillow exerts, in N? (Include gravity acting during the stop.)
solution: Impact speed is $v = \sqrt{2(9.8)(1.2)} = 4.85\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Over the stop, $(N - mg)\Delta t = mv$, so $N = mv/\Delta t + mg = 1.78 + 0.54 = 2.32\ \mathrm{N}$. A hard floor stopping the egg in $1\ \mathrm{ms}$ would need over $250\ \mathrm{N}$.

name: Recoil of a rifle
statement: A $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ rifle fires a $12\ \mathrm{g}$ bullet at $600\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the recoil speed of the rifle, in m/s?
solution: Total momentum starts at zero, so $M V = m v$: $V = (0.012)(600)/4.0 = 1.8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ backward.

name: Ball bouncing off the floor
statement: A $0.45\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball is dropped from $1.8\ \mathrm{m}$ and rebounds to $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$. What is the magnitude of the impulse the floor delivers, in N·s?
solution: Down: $v_1 = 5.94\ \mathrm{m/s}$; up: $v_2 = 4.85\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Because the direction flips, the speeds add: $J = m(v_1+v_2) = 0.45(10.79) = 4.86\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

name: Impulse at an angle
statement: A $0.16\ \mathrm{kg}$ puck moving east at $9.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is struck and afterwards moves north at $12\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the impulse, in N·s?
solution: Impulse is a vector: $\Delta \vec p = m(0,12) - m(9,0) = (-1.44, 1.92)\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. Its magnitude is $0.16\sqrt{81+144} = 2.4\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

name: Firehose reaction force
statement: A firefighter holds a hose delivering $25\ \mathrm{kg/s}$ of water at $22\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What backward force must she resist, in N?
solution: The hose gives the water momentum at a rate $\dot m v = 550\ \mathrm{N}$, and by Newton's third law the same force pushes back on the firefighter.

name: Sand into a cart
statement: Sand falls vertically into a cart at $8.0\ \mathrm{kg/s}$. The cart is pulled along at a constant $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ on frictionless rails. What horizontal force is needed, in N?
solution: Each kilogram of sand must be accelerated from $0$ to $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ horizontally: $F = v\,dm/dt = (3.0)(8.0) = 24\ \mathrm{N}$.

name: Two-dimensional impulse from gravity
statement: A $0.30\ \mathrm{kg}$ projectile is launched at $25\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $40^\circ$ and lands at the same height. What is the magnitude of the total impulse gravity delivered during the flight, in N·s?
solution: Flight time is $t = 2v_0\sin\theta/g = 2(25)(0.643)/9.8 = 3.28\ \mathrm{s}$. Then $J = mgt = (0.30)(9.8)(3.28) = 9.64\ \mathrm{N\,s}$, which equals the reversal of vertical momentum, $2mv_0\sin\theta$.

name: Karate chop
statement: A $0.70\ \mathrm{kg}$ hand moving at $11\ \mathrm{m/s}$ is stopped by a board in $3.0\ \mathrm{ms}$. What average force does the board feel, in N?
solution: $\bar F = m\Delta v/\Delta t = (0.70)(11)/0.0030 = 2567\ \mathrm{N}$. Short contact times are what make impacts violent.

name: Momentum of a system
statement: A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart moves east at $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and a $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart moves west at $2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the total momentum, in kg·m/s?
solution: Taking east as positive, $p = (3.0)(4.0) + (5.0)(-2.0) = 12 - 10 = 2.0\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ east.

name: Airbag versus dashboard
statement: In a crash a driver's stopping time increases from $0.020\ \mathrm{s}$ (dashboard) to $0.12\ \mathrm{s}$ (airbag) for the same change in momentum. By what factor is the average force reduced? (Give the pure number.)
solution: For fixed $\Delta p$, $\bar F \propto 1/\Delta t$. Stretching the stop by $0.12/0.020 = 6$ cuts the force by a factor of $6$.

name: Non-constant impact force
statement: During a collision a force $F(t) = F_0\sin(\pi t/T)$ acts, with $F_0 = 900\ \mathrm{N}$ and $T = 0.040\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the total impulse, in N·s?
solution: $J = \int_0^{T}F_0\sin(\pi t/T)\,dt = \frac{2F_0T}{\pi} = \frac{2(900)(0.040)}{\pi} = 22.9\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. Note the average force is $2F_0/\pi \approx 0.64F_0$.

name: Rocket in deep space
statement: A rocket of initial mass $2000\ \mathrm{kg}$ burns fuel with exhaust speed $2800\ \mathrm{m/s}$ until its mass is $800\ \mathrm{kg}$. Starting from rest in deep space, what is its final speed, in m/s?
solution: The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation gives $\Delta v = v_{\rm ex}\ln(m_i/m_f) = 2800\ln(2.5) = 2565\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Water jet that rebounds
statement: A jet of water, $6.0\ \mathrm{kg/s}$ at $10\ \mathrm{m/s}$, strikes a curved vane that turns it around completely so it leaves at $10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ in the opposite direction. What force does the water exert on the vane, in N?
solution: The momentum change rate is $\dot m(v - (-v)) = 2\dot m v = 2(6.0)(10) = 120\ \mathrm{N}$ — twice the force of a jet that simply stops.

name: Falling chain onto a scale
statement: A uniform chain of linear density $1.5\ \mathrm{kg/m}$ is dropped from rest so its lower end just touches a scale. When $0.80\ \mathrm{m}$ has landed, what does the scale read, in N?
solution: Two contributions: the weight of the chain already at rest, $\lambda y g = 11.76\ \mathrm{N}$, plus the force stopping the arriving links, $\lambda v^2 = \lambda(2gy) = 23.52\ \mathrm{N}$. The scale reads $35.3\ \mathrm{N}$, three times the resting weight of the landed portion.

name: Hovering by thrust
statement: A drone hovers by pushing air downward at $18\ \mathrm{m/s}$. If the drone plus payload weighs $32\ \mathrm{N}$, what mass of air must it push down per second, in kg/s?
solution: Hovering requires thrust equal to weight: $\dot m v = W$, so $\dot m = 32/18 = 1.78\ \mathrm{kg/s}$.

name: Impulse on a bouncing stream of balls
statement: A machine fires $20$ balls per second, each of mass $0.050\ \mathrm{kg}$, at $16\ \mathrm{m/s}$ against a wall; each rebounds at $12\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the average force on the wall, in N?
solution: Each ball changes momentum by $m(16+12) = 1.4\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. At $20$ balls per second the average force is $(20)(1.4) = 28\ \mathrm{N}$.

name: Rocket lifting off
statement: A rocket starts from rest on the launch pad and burns fuel at a constant rate so that its mass drops from $5000\ \mathrm{kg}$ to $2000\ \mathrm{kg}$ over $50\ \mathrm{s}$; the exhaust speed is $2400\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Ignoring drag but including gravity, what is its speed at burnout, in m/s?
solution: With gravity, $\Delta v = v_{\rm ex}\ln(m_i/m_f) - g t_b = 2400\ln(2.5) - (9.8)(50) = 2199 - 490 = 1709\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Rope pulled off a pile
statement: A rope of linear density $0.90\ \mathrm{kg/m}$ lies in a heap. One end is pulled horizontally at a constant $2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$, so more rope is set in motion each second. What horizontal force is required, in N?
solution: Each second, $\lambda v$ kilograms of rope must be brought from rest to $v$, so $F = \frac{d}{dt}(\lambda x v) = \lambda v^2 = (0.90)(4.0) = 3.6\ \mathrm{N}$. Half the work done goes into kinetic energy; the rest is lost in the jerk at the pile.

name: Carts that stick
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart at $6.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ collides with a stationary $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart and they stick together. What is their common speed, in m/s?
solution: Momentum is conserved: $(2.0)(6.0) = (6.0)v$, so $v = 2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Head-on stick
statement: A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block moving east at $5.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ hits a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block moving west at $2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$; they stick. What is the final speed, in m/s?
solution: $p_{\rm tot} = 15 - 4 = 11\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ east, and the total mass is $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$, so $v = 2.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ east.

name: Equal masses, elastic
statement: A $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball moving at $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ collides elastically head-on with an identical ball at rest. What is the speed of the first ball afterward, in m/s?
solution: For equal masses in a head-on elastic collision, the velocities simply swap. The incoming ball stops and the target leaves at $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Energy lost when sticking
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart at $6.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ sticks to a stationary $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart. How much kinetic energy is lost, in J?
solution: Before: $\tfrac12(2.0)(36) = 36\ \mathrm{J}$. After: $v = 2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$, so $\tfrac12(6.0)(4) = 12\ \mathrm{J}$. The loss is $24\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Explosion of a cart
statement: A $6.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart at rest explodes into a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ piece moving left at $9.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and a $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ piece. What is the speed of the $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ piece, in m/s?
solution: Total momentum stays zero: $(2.0)(9.0) = (4.0)v$, so $v = 4.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$ to the right.

name: Ballistic pendulum, first step
statement: A $20\ \mathrm{g}$ bullet at $300\ \mathrm{m/s}$ embeds in a $1.98\ \mathrm{kg}$ block at rest. What is the speed of the block-plus-bullet immediately after, in m/s?

name: Elastic with a wall
statement: A $0.30\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball hits a rigid wall head-on at $7.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and bounces back elastically. What is the magnitude of its momentum change, in kg·m/s?
solution: The speed is unchanged but the direction reverses: $|\Delta p| = 2mv = 2(0.30)(7.0) = 4.2\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.

name: Coefficient of restitution
statement: A ball dropped from $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ rebounds to $1.28\ \mathrm{m}$. What is the coefficient of restitution with the floor? (Give the pure number.)
solution: Speeds go as $\sqrt{h}$, so $e = v_{\rm up}/v_{\rm down} = \sqrt{h'/h} = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.80$.

name: Two skaters push off
statement: A $50\ \mathrm{kg}$ skater and a $75\ \mathrm{kg}$ skater push off from rest on frictionless ice. If the lighter one moves at $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$, how fast does the heavier one move, in m/s?
solution: Momentum stays zero: $(50)(3.0) = (75)v$, so $v = 2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Total momentum is conserved, energy is not
statement: Two lumps of clay, each $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$, moving toward each other at $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$, collide and stick. How much kinetic energy is lost, in J?
solution: The final momentum is zero, so the pair is at rest. All the initial kinetic energy, $2\times\tfrac12(0.50)(16) = 8.0\ \mathrm{J}$, is lost.

name: Elastic collision, unequal masses
statement: A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball at $5.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ collides elastically head-on with a stationary $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball. What is the final speed of the $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball, in m/s?
solution: For a head-on elastic collision with a target at rest, $v_2' = \frac{2m_1}{m_1+m_2}v_1 = \frac{6}{4}(5.0) = 7.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Heavy hits light: the projectile
statement: A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball at $5.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ hits a stationary $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball elastically head-on. What is the final velocity of the $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball, in m/s? (Positive means it keeps going forward.)
solution: $v_1' = \frac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}v_1 = \frac{2}{4}(5.0) = 2.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$: the heavier ball keeps moving forward, more slowly.

name: Light hits heavy
statement: A $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball moving at $8.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ strikes a stationary $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball elastically head-on. What is the final velocity of the light ball, in m/s? (Negative means it bounces back.)
solution: $v_1' = \frac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}v_1 = \frac{-3.5}{4.5}(8.0) = -6.22\ \mathrm{m/s}$: it rebounds, nearly at its original speed, as it would off a wall.

name: Ballistic pendulum height
statement: A $15\ \mathrm{g}$ bullet at $400\ \mathrm{m/s}$ embeds in a $2.985\ \mathrm{kg}$ block hanging from a string. How high does the block swing, in m?
solution: Momentum (not energy) applies during the embedding: $V = (0.015)(400)/3.000 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Then energy conservation on the swing: $h = V^2/2g = 4.0/19.6 = 0.204\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Fraction of energy lost
statement: A moving mass $m$ sticks to a stationary mass $3m$. What fraction of the original kinetic energy is lost? (Give the pure number.)
solution: Final speed is $v/4$, so $K_f/K_i = \frac{\tfrac12(4m)(v/4)^2}{\tfrac12 m v^2} = \tfrac14$. Three quarters of the energy is lost.

name: Two-dimensional stick
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ puck moving east at $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ collides and sticks to a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ puck moving north at $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the final speed, in m/s?
solution: Momentum components: $p_x = 6.0$, $p_y = 8.0\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, so $|p| = 10\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. Dividing by $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ gives $v = 2.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Direction after a 2D collision
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ puck moving east at $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ sticks to a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ puck moving north at $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What angle does the final velocity make with east, in degrees?
solution: $\tan\theta = p_y/p_x = 8.0/6.0$, so $\theta = 53.1^\circ$ north of east.

name: Equal-mass elastic in 2D
statement: On a frictionless table, a puck strikes an identical stationary puck a glancing elastic blow. If one leaves at $25^\circ$ from the original direction, at what angle does the other leave, in degrees?
solution: For equal masses in a two-dimensional elastic collision (both initially free, one at rest), the outgoing velocities are always perpendicular. So the second angle is $90^\circ - 25^\circ = 65^\circ$ on the other side.

name: Partially elastic collision
statement: A $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball at $6.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ hits a stationary $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball with coefficient of restitution $e = 0.60$. What is the final speed of the target ball, in m/s?
solution: With equal masses, momentum gives $v_1'+v_2' = 6.0$ and restitution gives $v_2'-v_1' = e(6.0) = 3.6$. Adding, $v_2' = 4.8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (and $v_1' = 1.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$).

name: Bullet passes through
statement: A $25\ \mathrm{g}$ bullet at $500\ \mathrm{m/s}$ passes through a $1.2\ \mathrm{kg}$ block resting on frictionless ice and exits at $200\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the block's speed afterward, in m/s?
solution: Momentum lost by the bullet is gained by the block: $(0.025)(500-200) = 7.5\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s} = (1.2)v$, so $v = 6.25\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Collision in the center-of-mass frame
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart at $9.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ approaches a $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart at rest. What is the speed of the center of mass, in m/s?
solution: $v_{\rm cm} = \frac{m_1v_1+m_2v_2}{m_1+m_2} = \frac{18}{6.0} = 3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. This is unchanged by the collision, whatever kind it is.

name: Maximum possible energy loss
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart at $9.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ collides with a $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart at rest. What is the largest amount of kinetic energy that can possibly be lost, in J?
solution: The maximum loss occurs when they move together at $v_{\rm cm} = 3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$: $K_i = 81\ \mathrm{J}$, $K_f = 27\ \mathrm{J}$, loss $= 54\ \mathrm{J}$. This equals the kinetic energy in the center-of-mass frame.

name: Superball on a basketball
statement: A tiny superball sits on top of a basketball. Both are dropped from $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and the basketball bounces elastically off the floor, then collides elastically with the much lighter superball. In the limit that the superball's mass is negligible, how high does the superball rise, in m?
solution: Both hit the floor at $v = \sqrt{2gh}$. The basketball rebounds at $+v$ while the superball is still moving at $-v$. In the basketball's frame the superball approaches at $2v$ and, in an elastic bounce off a much heavier body, leaves at $+2v$ in that frame — i.e. $3v$ in the lab. Height goes as $v^2$, so it rises $9h = 9.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Two blocks and a spring
statement: A $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block moving at $6.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ hits a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block at rest that carries an ideal spring. What is the maximum energy stored in the spring, in J?
solution: The spring is most compressed when both blocks move together at $v_{\rm cm} = 2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Then $U_{\max} = K_i - K_{\rm cm} = 18 - 6 = 12\ \mathrm{J}$.

name: Oblique elastic collision with a wall
statement: A $0.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ puck strikes a smooth wall at $30^\circ$ from the wall's normal, at $9.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$, and rebounds elastically. What is the magnitude of the impulse on the puck, in N·s?
solution: A smooth wall changes only the normal component of velocity, reversing it. So $|J| = 2mv\cos\theta = 2(0.20)(9.0)(0.866) = 3.12\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

name: Recoil angle in a 2D collision
statement: A $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass moving east at $5.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ strikes a $6.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass at rest. Afterward the $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass moves at $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $40^\circ$ north of east. What is the speed of the $6.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass, in m/s?
solution: Conserve each component: $p_x = 20 - 12\cos40^\circ = 10.81$, $p_y = -12\sin40^\circ = -7.71\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. The magnitude is $13.28$, so $v = 13.28/6.0 = 2.21\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Repeated bounces
statement: A ball with coefficient of restitution $e = 0.75$ is dropped from $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$. What is the total vertical distance it travels before coming to rest, in m?
solution: After each bounce the height is multiplied by $e^2 = 0.5625$. The total path is $h + 2h(e^2 + e^4 + \cdots) = h\left(1 + \frac{2e^2}{1-e^2}\right) = 2.0(1+2.571) = 7.14\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Maximum deflection of a heavy projectile
statement: A $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball collides elastically with a stationary $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball. What is the maximum possible angle by which the heavy ball can be deflected, in degrees?
solution: For $m_1 > m_2$ the projectile can never be scattered by more than $\theta_{\max}$ where $\sin\theta_{\max} = m_2/m_1$. Here $\sin\theta_{\max} = 0.40$, so $\theta_{\max} = 23.6^\circ$.

name: Neutron moderation
statement: A neutron (mass $1.0\ \mathrm{u}$) makes a head-on elastic collision with a carbon nucleus (mass $12\ \mathrm{u}$) at rest. What fraction of its kinetic energy does the neutron lose? (Give the pure number.)
solution: For a head-on elastic collision, the fraction of energy transferred is $\frac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1+m_2)^2} = \frac{4(1)(12)}{169} = 0.284$. Hydrogen ($m_2 = m_1$) would transfer all of it, which is why hydrogen-rich materials are good moderators.

name: Three-body explosion
statement: A stationary $9.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ shell bursts into three pieces. A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ piece flies east at $8.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ piece flies north at $6.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the speed of the remaining $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ piece, in m/s?
solution: Total momentum stays zero, so the third piece carries $(-24, -12)\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{576+144} = 26.83$, so $v = 26.83/4.0 = 6.71\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Two masses on a line
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass sits at $x=0$ and a $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass at $x = 5.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Where is the center of mass, in m?
solution: $x_{\rm cm} = \frac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i} = \frac{(2)(0)+(3)(5.0)}{5.0} = 3.0\ \mathrm{m}$: closer to the heavier mass.

name: Dumbbell
statement: Two equal $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ balls sit at $x = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and $x = 4.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Where is the center of mass, in m?
solution: For equal masses the center of mass is at the midpoint: $x_{\rm cm} = (1.0+4.0)/2 = 2.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Three masses
statement: Masses $1.0$, $2.0$, and $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ sit at $x = 0$, $2.0$, and $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Where is the center of mass, in m?

name: Uniform rod
statement: A uniform rod of length $2.4\ \mathrm{m}$ lies along the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2.4\ \mathrm{m}$. Where is its center of mass, in m?
solution: For a uniform rod the center of mass is at the geometric center, $x = 1.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Center of mass in two dimensions
statement: A $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass at $(0,0)$ and a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass at $(4.0, 6.0)\ \mathrm{m}$. What is the $y$-coordinate of the center of mass, in m?
solution: Equal masses put the center of mass at the midpoint: $y_{\rm cm} = 3.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Earth-Moon system
statement: Earth has mass $5.97\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and the Moon $7.35\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{kg}$, separated by $3.84\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$. How far from Earth's center is the system's center of mass, in m?
solution: $x_{\rm cm} = \frac{m_M d}{m_E+m_M} = \frac{(7.35\times10^{22})(3.84\times10^{8})}{6.043\times10^{24}} = 4.67\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$ — inside Earth, whose radius is $6.37\times10^6\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Center-of-mass velocity
statement: A $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart moves east at $4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and a $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart moves east at $8.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the speed of their center of mass, in m/s?

name: Two-particle center of mass shifts
statement: A $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass at $x=0$ and a $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass at $x = 10\ \mathrm{m}$. If the light mass moves to $x = 5.0\ \mathrm{m}$, how far does the center of mass move, in m?
solution: Initially $x_{\rm cm} = 10/5 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$; afterward $x_{\rm cm} = 5/5 = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$. The shift is $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Momentum from the center of mass
statement: A system of total mass $12\ \mathrm{kg}$ has a center of mass moving at $2.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the system's total momentum, in kg·m/s?
solution: $\vec P_{\rm tot} = M\vec v_{\rm cm} = (12)(2.5) = 30\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, always exactly true.

name: Balancing a seesaw
statement: A $30\ \mathrm{kg}$ child sits $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ from a pivot. How far on the other side must a $40\ \mathrm{kg}$ child sit so the center of mass is over the pivot, in m?
solution: Balance requires $m_1d_1 = m_2d_2$: $d_2 = (30)(2.0)/40 = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: L-shaped plate
statement: A uniform L-shaped plate is made of two rectangles: one $4.0\ \mathrm{m}\times1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ with its lower-left corner at the origin lying along $x$, and one $1.0\ \mathrm{m}\times3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ sitting on top of the left end (from $x=0$ to $1.0$, $y=1.0$ to $4.0$). What is the $x$-coordinate of the center of mass, in m?
solution: Treat each rectangle as a point mass at its own center, weighted by area. Areas $4.0$ and $3.0\ \mathrm{m^2}$ at $x = 2.0$ and $0.5\ \mathrm{m}$: $x_{\rm cm} = (8.0+1.5)/7.0 = 1.36\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: L-shaped plate, vertical position
statement: For the same L-shaped plate (a $4.0\times1.0$ rectangle along the bottom plus a $1.0\times3.0$ rectangle stacked on its left end from $y=1.0$ to $4.0$), what is the $y$-coordinate of the center of mass, in m?
solution: Centers are at $y = 0.5$ and $y = 2.5\ \mathrm{m}$, weighted by areas $4.0$ and $3.0$: $y_{\rm cm} = (2.0+7.5)/7.0 = 1.36\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Nonuniform rod
statement: A rod of length $3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ has linear density $\lambda = 2x$ (kg/m, $x$ in meters from one end). Where is its center of mass, in m?
solution: $x_{\rm cm} = \frac{\int_0^{L}x\lambda\,dx}{\int_0^{L}\lambda\,dx} = \frac{\tfrac23 L^3}{L^2} = \tfrac23 L = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$. The heavier end pulls it past the midpoint.

name: Rod with density growing as x squared
statement: A rod of length $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ has $\lambda = 3x^2$ (kg/m). Where is its center of mass, in m?
solution: $x_{\rm cm} = \frac{\int_0^L x\cdot 3x^2dx}{\int_0^L 3x^2dx} = \frac{(3/4)L^4}{L^3} = \tfrac34 L = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Disk with a hole
statement: A uniform disk of radius $R = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ centered at the origin has a circular hole of radius $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ cut out, centered at $x = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Where is the center of mass of what remains, in m? (Give the $x$-coordinate; negative means left of the origin.)
solution: Treat the hole as negative mass: $x_{\rm cm} = \frac{A(0) - a(1.0)}{A-a}$ with $A = 4\pi$ and $a = 0.25\pi$. This gives $x_{\rm cm} = -0.25/3.75 = -0.0667\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Center of mass of a triangle
statement: A uniform triangular plate has vertices at $(0,0)$, $(6.0,0)$, and $(0,3.0)$ meters. What is the $x$-coordinate of its center of mass, in m?
solution: The centroid of a triangle is the average of its vertices: $x_{\rm cm} = (0+6.0+0)/3 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Person walking on a boat
statement: A $60\ \mathrm{kg}$ person stands at one end of a $120\ \mathrm{kg}$, $4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ boat floating on still water. He walks to the other end. How far does the boat move, in m?
solution: With no external horizontal force, the center of mass cannot move. If the boat shifts $d$, the person shifts $4.0-d$ the other way: $60(4.0-d) = 120d$, so $d = 240/180 = 1.33\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Center of mass acceleration
statement: Two blocks of $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ interact through a spring while a single external force of $16\ \mathrm{N}$ pushes on the $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block. What is the acceleration of the center of mass, in m/s²?
solution: Internal spring forces cancel, so $\vec a_{\rm cm} = \vec F_{\rm ext}/M_{\rm tot} = 16/8.0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, whatever the spring is doing.

name: Exploding projectile
statement: A projectile launched from the ground explodes at the top of its arc, $80\ \mathrm{m}$ downrange, into two equal pieces. One piece falls straight down from the explosion point. Where does the other land, measured from the launch point, in m?
solution: Without the explosion the projectile would land at $160\ \mathrm{m}$, and the center of mass follows that path regardless. With one half at $80\ \mathrm{m}$, the other must satisfy $\tfrac12(80)+\tfrac12 x = 160$, giving $x = 240\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Center of mass of the Sun-Jupiter system
statement: The Sun has mass $1.99\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$, Jupiter $1.90\times10^{27}\ \mathrm{kg}$, and they are $7.78\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m}$ apart. How far is the center of mass from the Sun's center, in m?
solution: $x_{\rm cm} = \frac{m_J d}{m_S+m_J} = \frac{(1.90\times10^{27})(7.78\times10^{11})}{1.992\times10^{30}} = 7.42\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$, slightly outside the Sun's radius of $6.96\times10^8\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Two carts and a compressed spring
statement: On frictionless rails a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and a $6.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ cart are pushed apart by a spring, both starting at rest. When the light cart has moved $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$, how far has the heavy cart moved, in m?
solution: The center of mass stays put: $m_1d_1 = m_2d_2$, so $d_2 = (2.0)(0.60)/6.0 = 0.20\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Semicircular wire
statement: A uniform wire is bent into a semicircle of radius $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$. How far from the center of the circle is its center of mass, in m?
solution: For a semicircular arc the center of mass lies at $2R/\pi$ from the center, along the symmetry axis: $2(0.40)/\pi = 0.255\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Semicircular plate
statement: A uniform semicircular plate (half-disk) has radius $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$. How far from the center of the straight edge is its center of mass, in m?
solution: Integrating strips of a half-disk gives $y_{\rm cm} = \frac{4R}{3\pi} = \frac{4(0.60)}{3\pi} = 0.255\ \mathrm{m}$ — closer in than the $2R/\pi$ of a semicircular wire, since a disk has more area near the flat edge.

name: Solid cone
statement: A uniform solid cone has height $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$. How far above the base is its center of mass, in m?
solution: Slices at height $z$ have area $\propto (h-z)^2$. Integrating gives $z_{\rm cm} = h/4 = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ above the base.

name: Hemispherical bowl versus solid hemisphere
statement: A uniform solid hemisphere has radius $0.80\ \mathrm{m}$. How far from the flat face is its center of mass, in m?
solution: For a solid hemisphere, $z_{\rm cm} = 3R/8 = 3(0.80)/8 = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. (A thin hemispherical shell would give $R/2$.)

name: Stacked blocks overhang
statement: Two identical uniform blocks of length $L = 0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ are stacked at the edge of a table, each shifted to maximize overhang without toppling. What is the maximum total overhang beyond the table edge, in m?
solution: The top block can overhang the one below by $L/2$; the pair's combined center of mass must be over the table edge, allowing another $L/4$. Total overhang is $3L/4 = 0.225\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Where the rocket's pieces land
statement: A $6.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ firework at the top of its flight, $100\ \mathrm{m}$ downrange, splits into a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ piece that lands at $60\ \mathrm{m}$ and a $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ piece. The unexploded firework would have landed at $200\ \mathrm{m}$. Where does the $4.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ piece land, in m?
solution: The center of mass follows the original parabola and lands at $200\ \mathrm{m}$: $6(200) = 2(60) + 4x$, so $x = (1200-120)/4 = 270\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Chain hanging over a pulley
statement: A uniform chain of total length $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and mass $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ hangs over a small frictionless pulley with $1.4\ \mathrm{m}$ on one side and $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ on the other. How far below the pulley is the chain's center of mass, in m?
solution: Each hanging segment has its own center at half its length: $\lambda = 2.5\ \mathrm{kg/m}$ gives masses $3.5$ and $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ at depths $0.70$ and $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. Then $y_{\rm cm} = (2.45+0.45)/5.0 = 0.58\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Man climbing a rope over a pulley
statement: A $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ man hangs from one side of a rope over a frictionless pulley, balanced by a $70\ \mathrm{kg}$ counterweight on the other side. He climbs the rope at $0.50\ \mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the rope. What is the speed of the center of mass of the man-plus-counterweight system, in m/s?
solution: Because the masses are equal and the rope is inextensible, whatever the man does the counterweight mirrors: they move at equal speeds in opposite senses relative to the ground. Their center of mass therefore stays at rest, $v_{\rm cm} = 0$.

name: Center of mass of a hollow tapered rod
statement: A rod of length $4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ has linear density $\lambda(x) = \lambda_0(1 + x/L)$ with $x$ measured from one end and $L = 4.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Where is its center of mass, in m?
solution: With $\lambda = \lambda_0(1+x/L)$, the mass is $\lambda_0 L(1+\tfrac12) = 1.5\lambda_0 L$ and $\int x\lambda\,dx = \lambda_0 L^2(\tfrac12+\tfrac13) = \tfrac56\lambda_0 L^2$. So $x_{\rm cm} = \frac{5L}{9} = 2.22\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Revolutions to radians
statement: A wheel turns through $3.5$ revolutions. What is that angle in radians?
solution: One revolution is $2\pi$ radians, so $\theta = 3.5(2\pi) = 21.99\ \mathrm{rad}$.

name: RPM to rad/s
statement: A motor spins at $1800\ \mathrm{rpm}$. What is its angular speed, in rad/s?
solution: $\omega = 1800\times\frac{2\pi}{60} = 188.5\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

name: Rim speed
statement: A wheel of radius $0.35\ \mathrm{m}$ spins at $20\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. What is the speed of a point on the rim, in m/s?

name: Angular acceleration
statement: A turntable speeds up from $2.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ to $11\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ in $3.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What is its angular acceleration, in rad/s²?
solution: $\alpha = \Delta\omega/\Delta t = 9.0/3.0 = 3.0\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$.

name: Angle turned at constant alpha
statement: A disk starts from rest and has angular acceleration $4.0\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$. Through what angle does it turn in $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$, in rad?
solution: $\theta = \tfrac12\alpha t^2 = \tfrac12(4.0)(25) = 50\ \mathrm{rad}$.

name: Centripetal acceleration on a rim
statement: A point $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ from the axis of a wheel spinning at $30\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. What is its centripetal acceleration, in m/s²?

name: Bicycle wheel distance
statement: A bicycle wheel of radius $0.34\ \mathrm{m}$ makes $40$ complete turns. How far does the bicycle travel, in m?
solution: Each turn advances the bike by one circumference, $2\pi R$: $d = 40(2\pi)(0.34) = 85.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

name: Stopping a flywheel
